issues.legal_issue: An appellant may not obtain consideration of an alleged omission by the High Court merely by asserting that an argument was raised but not considered.
material_facts: In the appeal, the appellant alleged that the High Court had not considered a number of arguments.
The High Court's judgment addressed the factual and legal issues, and the appellant had not established that the alleged omissions were admitted or demonstrable.
The appellant had not obtained an order from the High Court on any material point said to have escaped scrutiny before its judgment was signed.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court declined to entertain the alleged omissions and deprecated the practice of making such allegations without first raising the omission before the High Court and obtaining its order.
issues.legal_principle: The High Court is a Court of Record. Unless an omission is admitted or demonstrably proved, the Supreme Court will not investigate an allegation that the High Court failed to consider an argument. A material point said to have escaped scrutiny should be brought to the High Court's attention before judgment is signed, and an order on that submission should be obtained before raising it on appeal.

rule.if: supreme_court_appeal and appellant_alleges_omitted_argument and (omission_not_admitted and omission_not_demonstrated)

predicates.supreme_court_appeal: The matter is an appeal before the Supreme Court from a High Court decision.
predicates.appellant_alleges_omitted_argument: The appellant claims that the High Court did not consider an argument raised before it.
predicates.omission_not_admitted: The High Court has not admitted that it omitted to consider the argument.
predicates.omission_not_demonstrated: The appellant has not demonstrably established that the High Court omitted to consider the argument.

issues.definition: When an appellant in a Supreme Court appeal alleges an unadmitted and unproved omission by the High Court, the Supreme Court declines to entertain that allegation.

issues.legal_issue: A removal power conferred on a supervisory body by an amendment may be exercised on the basis of disobedience that occurred before the amendment took effect.
material_facts: The appellant was a Mutwalli subject to the supervisory body's authority.
The appellant had disobeyed the body's orders and directions before the amendment transferred the removal power to the body itself.
The body removed the appellant after the amendment took effect, relying on the earlier disobedience.
The amendment changed who could exercise the removal power, and the earlier proceedings concerning the alleged misconduct were already underway.
issues.conclusion: The supervisory body could exercise its amended removal power on the basis of orders and directions disobeyed before the amendment took effect.
issues.legal_principle: A statute is not necessarily retrospective merely because a power conferred by it is based on earlier conduct, where the power is intended to reach that conduct. The Court also held that there was no vested right to continue as Mutawalli after mismanagement and misconduct had been established. It applied the amended removal provision of the Bihar Waqfs Act, 1947, as amended by the Bihar Waqfs (Amendment) Act, 1951.

predicates.waqf_mutawalli_removal_case: The proceeding concerns removal of a Mutawalli in the administration of a waqf.
predicates.amended_law_transfers_removal_power_to_s: A later amendment gives the supervisory body itself authority to remove the Mutawalli.
predicates.prior_supervisory_orders_were_disobeyed: The Mutawalli disobeyed the supervisory body's orders or directions before the amendment took effect.

issues.definition: If an amendment transfers removal authority to a supervisory body in a waqf Mutawalli removal case, and the Mutawalli had already disobeyed that body's orders or directions, the body may rely on that prior disobedience to remove the Mutawalli.

issues.legal_issue: Disobedience of an order issued before an amendment can support removal under the amended power even if the earlier provision referred to directions rather than orders.
material_facts: Before the amendment, the earlier removal provision referred to disobedience of directions.
The appellant contended that disobedience of orders issued before the amendment could not support removal under the amended provision, which referred to orders and directions.
The Court treated orders and directions as expressions of the binding wish of the supervisory body, differing in degree.
issues.conclusion: The appellant's distinction between orders and directions did not prevent reliance on disobedience of an earlier order as a ground for removal.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that orders and directions both express the binding wish of the supervisory body, although an order is more peremptory. It rejected an interpretation under which disobedience of a direction could lead to removal but disobedience of an order would go unpunished, applying the removal provision of the Bihar Waqfs Act, 1947, as amended in 1951.

predicates.waqf_mutawalli_removal_case: The proceeding concerns removal of a Mutawalli in the administration of a waqf.
predicates.amended_removal_power_covers_orders_and_: The applicable removal power treats disobedience of orders and directions from the supervisory body as grounds for removal.
predicates.prior_supervisory_order_was_disobeyed: The Mutawalli disobeyed an order issued by the supervisory body before the amended removal power took effect.

issues.definition: When a Mutawalli removal proceeding involves an amended power covering disobedience of orders and directions, prior disobedience of an order can support removal.

issues.legal_issue: The chairperson may exercise the supervisory body's powers where immediate action is necessary and a meeting cannot be arranged in time, and may also exercise powers delegated to the chairperson.
material_facts: The chairperson ordered the appellant's removal after the appellant failed to deposit money found due to the waqf.
The lower courts concurrently found that immediate removal and taking control of the waqf property were necessary.
The chairperson reported the action to the supervisory body, which approved it.
The Act provided for exercise of the body's powers by the chairperson in an emergency and for delegation of powers to the chairperson.
issues.conclusion: The chairperson had authority to act, and the appellant's objection to the chairperson exercising the body's removal power was rejected.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 37 and 38 of the Bihar Waqfs Act, 1947, respectively allow the chairperson to exercise a power of the supervisory body when immediate action is necessary and a meeting cannot be arranged in time, and permit the body to delegate its powers and duties to the chairperson in specified circumstances. The Court relied on the concurrent finding that immediate action was necessary and on the body's subsequent approval.

predicates.waqf_mutawalli_removal_case: The proceeding concerns removal of a Mutawalli in the administration of a waqf.
predicates.immediate_action_was_necessary: The circumstances required the supervisory body to act immediately to protect the waqf or its property.
predicates.supervisory_body_meeting_could_not_be_ar: A meeting of the supervisory body could not be arranged in time to take the necessary action.

issues.definition: If immediate action is necessary in a waqf Mutawalli removal case and the supervisory body cannot meet in time, the chairperson may exercise the body's power.

issues.legal_issue: A temporary Mutawalli appointed by the supervisory body does not require prior permission or subsequent ratification by a court merely because the appointment is subject to a contrary court order.
material_facts: After removing the appellant, the supervisory body appointed another person as temporary Mutawalli.
The appointment was challenged on the ground that it required ratification by the District Judge.
The High Court held that the statutory language made the appointment effective according to its terms unless a competent court ordered otherwise.
issues.conclusion: The temporary appointment did not require prior permission or subsequent assent by the District Judge and remained effective subject to a contrary order by a competent court.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 32 of the Bihar Waqfs Act, 1947, the supervisory body could make a temporary appointment when the office of Mutawalli was vacant. The words making the appointment subject to an order of the competent court meant that it would endure according to its terms until a contrary court order, not that prior permission or subsequent assent was required.

predicates.waqf_management_case: The proceeding concerns the management of a waqf and the Mutawalli's office.
predicates.supervisory_body_appoints_temporary_muta: The supervisory body appoints a person temporarily to the office of Mutawalli.
predicates.appointment_is_subject_to_contrary_court: The appointment is expressed to remain subject to any contrary order by a competent court.

issues.definition: When the supervisory body makes a temporary appointment subject to a contrary court order, the appointment needs no prior permission or subsequent ratification.
